title: Reading Comprehension Is Not a Skill
author: Carl Hendrick
summary: Drawing on eighteen years teaching English, Hendrick argues that reading comprehension is not a generic, teachable skill but the product of vocabulary and background knowledge, and that strategy instruction built the curriculum from the symptoms of comprehension failure rather than its cause. He uses a recent reanalysis showing cognitive and metacognitive strategies shrink to near-zero effects on standardised tests, while siding with Mullins' critique that the same paper mishandled content instruction, noting that knowledge-building was the only approach whose effect grew with duration. He frames knowledge-building not as an intervention to be tested in short trials but as an 'instructional invariant', citing Core Knowledge results that closed income gaps after four years. He then concedes that naive direct vocabulary teaching does not generalise, because coverage thresholds of 95-99 per cent make word-by-word instruction 'drops in an ocean'. His answer is generative, morphology-based instruction, illustrated through the Word Mapping Project's matrices and robust encounters, which showed transfer to untaught words. He closes by casting the vocabulary gap as an equity problem, since for disadvantaged pupils the school curriculum is the main source of the words and knowledge comprehension depends on.
points: Comprehension strategies like 'finding the main idea' are labels for failure turned into curriculum; the strategy sits downstream of knowing what the words mean.

On standardised measures, cognitive strategy instruction showed an effect of only 0.09 and gains plateau after roughly ten hours, while content instruction was the only approach whose effect grew with duration.
Knowledge-building should be treated as a continuous condition for learning rather than a dosed intervention, so short RCTs systematically undervalue it.

Direct teaching of Tier 2 word lists does not generalise to untaught vocabulary, but morphology instruction (prefixes, roots, suffixes) is generative and produced gains on words never explicitly taught.
Because advantaged children absorb vocabulary at home, a knowledge-rich curriculum is inherently compensatory and the vocabulary gap is fundamentally an equity issue.
quotes: I taught English and reading comprehension for eighteen years. One thing I learned slowly, and against the grain of almost everything I was trained to do, is that when a student cannot grasp the main idea of a passage, the problem is almost never that they lack a “strategy.” The problem is that they do not understand enough of the words.

We built an entire instructional architecture from the symptoms of the problem rather than from its cause. The description of what students could not do was mistaken for an explanation of why they could not do it.

Strategies are not a deep competence that rewards sustained practice; they are a thin procedural layer that maxes out almost immediately. When you strip away the researcher-created measures, the flattering proximal tests, the assessments designed to detect exactly what was taught, strategy instruction produces almost nothing on the measures that matter.

But knowledge does not work like a treatment. It compounds. It accretes. It builds the very architecture through which future comprehension becomes possible. To measure it as though it were a pill is to fundamentally misunderstand the mechanism.

If a student needs to know 98 per cent of the words in a passage, and they are encountering academic texts with thousands of distinct word forms, and direct instruction of individual words does not generalise beyond the words taught, then the gap cannot be closed one word at a time.

Morphological instruction generates transfer because it teaches the underlying code, not individual items. A student who understands that sect means “cut” and that -ion makes a noun does not need to be explicitly taught dissection.

The students most harmed by the strategy-heavy, knowledge-light approach are the ones who arrive at school with the smallest vocabularies. They are the ones for whom the school curriculum is not a supplement but a lifeline: the primary means by which they will acquire the words and the knowledge that make comprehension possible.
